title: KV shadowing, snapshotting and prefetch handoff deep dive - Terrabay Systems
summary: Deep technical sync on KV cache shadowing and snapshotting to reduce cold-start paging during long-context sessions. Discussed LRU vs generational eviction, multitenant interference, on-prem VPC bandwidth impact, and telemetry required to tune prefetch handoff. Agreed to run a small pilot with snapshotting enabled on an isolated tenant and share trace/telemetry collection plan.
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-01-30
Start: 16:00 PST
Duration: ~57m
Recording: yes
Notes: rough transcript, some ASR errors

[00:00:00] Maya (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intros? We'll focus on the KV shadowing/snapshotting design and prefetch handoff, and how that interacts with your on-prem setup.

[00:00:18] Carlos (Customer): Hi, Carlos here. We're seeing periodic lat spikes and paging when customers go into long-doc summarizations. It's like the tokenstore empties and we get big tails.

[00:00:28] Liam (SE): Ok noted. Can you describe the pattern? Is it sustained long sequences or bursty long sequences?

[00:00:35] Priya: Mostly bursty — users open up 30k-token contexts occasionally for chains of thought, not every request. The problem is the first few minutes after a rare long context triggers heavy KV load and we see prefetch thrash.

[00:00:48] Maya: Right — we're thinking about two complementary approaches: lightweight shadowing + on-demand snapshotting of hot prefixes, and improving the prefetch handoff so it doesn't evict cold prefixes prematurely.

[00:01:05] Evelyn: When you say snapshotting, do you mean persist to SSD then warm into memory or keep an in-memory compressed checkpoint?

[00:01:14] Liam: Good question. Two modes: 1) disk-backed snapshotting — periodically materialize a compressed prefix blob to local NVMe and fetch into RAM on first access; 2) in-memory compressed snapshots using quantized KV representations (lower precision) to save residency. Both have tradeoffs.

[00:01:36] Jamal: On our VPC/on-prem nodes, networked storage is slow — NVMe is ok but snapshotting to NFS hurts. So we prefer in-memory if the memory hit is acceptable. But our SLOs on memory per-tenant are strict.

[00:01:52] Carlos: The eviction appears correlated with multi-tenant spikes. Tenant A will flush hot prefixes, then Tenant B comes and pollutes cache. Is there support for per-tenant quotas or generational eviction?

[00:02:05] Liam: We have per-tenant residency quotas and LRU by default. Generation-based eviction (young/old tiers) can help keep long-lived prefixes sticky. Shadowing can also keep a compressed copy in a slow tier so the hot tier stays high-performance.

[00:02:20] Priya: Can you walk through a timeline example? Say user triggers a 25k sequence — what's the flow with snapshotting enabled?

[00:02:28] Liam: Sure — (1) classifier marks prefix hot as it grows; (2) background snapshot worker compresses a snapshot to the slow tier or in-memory compressed store; (3) prefetcher parallel-fetches adjacent KV shards into primary memory; (4) handoff: when prefetch completes, the runtime increments a priority bit, preventing immediate eviction; (5) after steady state, the shadowed compressed copy may be garbage-collected.

[00:02:58] Carlos: Sounds good but the hitch point is the prefetch window: if prefetch is slow, the active working set will thrash. What telemetry should we collect to tune it?

[00:03:07] Maya: We recommend sequence-length histograms, per-prefix hit/miss rate, eviction wait time, snapshot throughput (MB/s), prefetch latency distribution (p50/p95/p99), and local NVMe vs network pull times. Also track memory residency per-tenant and cross-tenant eviction events.

[00:03:28] Evelyn: We can expose those metrics but need guidance on dashboard thresholds.

[00:03:34] Liam: We'll share a dashboard template. Quick rule-of-thumb: if p95 prefetch > 200ms and eviction rate > 5% for hot prefixes, you likely need to raise snapshot priority or increase compressed-tier memory.

[00:03:48] Priya: What about batching? Our current runtime does continuous batching which helps throughput but increases peak token-in-flight and amplifies KV load. Any suggestions?

[00:03:57] Sofia (PM): We discussed adaptive batching — shrink batch size during prefetch bursts, or enable per-prefix throttling so a single large sequence doesn't monopolize the batch. There's also hybrid batching: prefer small latency batches for long-context requests.

[00:04:12] Jamal: Does quantization affect KV correctness? We worry about degraded attention results if KV values are quantized aggressively.

[00:04:19] Liam: We've tested 8-bit and 4-bit quantized KV payloads. 8-bit is usually safe; 4-bit sometimes introduces subtle context degradation depending on model sensitivity. You can do lossy compressions for cold prefixes and keep full precision for head-of-prefix contexts.

[00:04:40] Carlos: Are there automatic fallback policies if a compressed snapshot yields bad quality?

[00:04:45] Maya: Yes, runtime can detect quality regressions by sampling generated outputs against a golden prompt set — if drift exceeds threshold, it transparently pulls full-precision KV for subsequent requests. We'll show an eval config.

[00:04:58] Priya: On the operational side, what about crash recovery? If node restarts, will snapshots speed warm start?

[00:05:06] Liam: Exactly — snapshots reduce warmup time. Instead of replaying full sequences to rebuild KV, the node loads the compressed snapshot and resumes with far fewer KV misses. For on-prem, ensure snapshot store has low-latency access or use a local ephemeral NVMe store.

[00:05:21] Evelyn: Any security implications for snapshot storage? We need encryption at rest and KMS integration.

[00:05:26] Maya: Snapshots obey the same encryption policy as model weights and logs — KMS/HSM integration for Private deployments, access controls, and audit logs. We'll attach our security whitepaper.

[00:05:36] Carlos: Let's talk about prefix reuse detection. We get high cardinality prefixes with minor edits — the cache treats them as distinct and that hurts hit rate.

[00:05:45] Liam: We can implement fuzzy-prefix hashing — normalize whitespace, small token edits, and apply a locality-sensitive hash to group near-identical prefixes. That increases reuse but risks merging semantically distinct contexts. It's a tradeoff.

[00:05:59] Priya: What about TTL / expiry heuristics? Some prefixes are ephemeral and should be low priority.

[00:06:06] Liam: True. Use activity-based TTLs: if a prefix hasn't been accessed in X minutes and isn't part of a pinned rollout, degrade it in generation. Also expose a pinning API for enterprise customers to pin prefixes during a POC.

[00:06:20] Maya: Back to multitenancy — suggestion: soft isolation with quotas plus a fast-path fair-queue in the prefetcher. If one tenant's prefetch saturates I/O, throttle it.

[00:06:30] Jamal: Our network egress in VPC is bumpy. Sometimes pulls for NVMe fill up NIC and affect other services. Can Redwood prioritize NIC usage?

[00:06:40] Liam: On Private, we expose NIC priority knobs and batch prefetch I/O by tenant with configurable concurrency. On Hosted we do automatic shaping. For on-prem, we can instrument an RPC backpressure to slow prefetch.

[00:06:54] Carlos: Implementation timeline — what's a minimal viable pilot for us?

[00:06:58] Maya: Recommend: (1) enable compressed snapshots in read-only mode for an isolated test tenant, (2) collect telemetry for 2 weeks using the dashboard template, (3) run A/B quality checks on golden prompts, (4) iterate eviction/generation policy. We can do this on your Private cluster or on a Redwood Dedicated pool.

[00:07:18] Priya: Storage: we'll provision a local NVMe for snapshots and keep limits.

[00:07:22] Evelyn: Sounds good. Who's owning which tasks?

[00:07:26] Maya: We'll capture action items.

[00:07:30] [--- mid-call technical deep dive continues with a few interruptions and faster back-and-forths ---]

[00:25:12] Liam: A couple of implementation notes: we recommend a 3-tier cache model: hot (full precision RAM), warm (in-memory compressed), cold (NVMe snapshot). Eviction moves items down tiers not immediately out. That reduces p99 fetch latency.

[00:25:38] Carlos: If we adopt generational GC, do we keep a reference age per-prefix? That adds metadata overhead.

[00:25:45] Liam: Yes, we keep a small 8-bit age counter per prefix and a hotness score. Overhead is minor compared to KV payload size.

[00:26:00] Priya: Any existing customers running this in prod?

[00:26:04] Maya: A handful of early enterprise customers are testing shadowing+snapshotting in Dedicated clusters; preliminary results show 40-60% reduction in cold-start p95 for long-context workloads. We'll anonymize and share a case study.

[00:26:18] Jamal: What about debug traces — we need sample request->KV timeline traces to pinpoint the eviction handoff.

[00:26:25] Liam: We have tracing hooks that record per-request KV lookups, misses, prefetch times, and snapshot loads. We'll supply a minimal collector that streams traces to your observability pipeline.

[00:26:38] Carlos: Can we get a copy of the proposed config YAML?

[00:26:41] Maya: Yes, we'll attach a sample config and a prefetch policy doc.

[00:26:47] Priya: Any gotchas with quantized compressed snapshots and replaying?

[00:26:52] Liam: Watch for accumulation error when recombining quantized KV across many steps — it's safer to keep head-of-prefix at full precision. Also, don't apply lossy compression to instruction tokens that control behavior.

[00:27:06] Evelyn: Ok, security again — snapshot access needs to be logged; on our side the auditor will need proof.

[00:27:12] Maya: We'll provide audit logs and KMS key rotation notes.

[00:27:20] [00:27:20] Maya: Quick recap?

[00:27:22] Carlos: Pilot with compressed snapshots on isolated tenant, collect telemetry, pin a handful of golden prompts, run A/B.

[00:27:29] Priya: We'll provision NVMe and open firewall rules for the test cluster.

[00:27:33] Liam: Redwood will provide config, dashboard template, and trace collector. We'll also include an eval harness for quality checks.

[00:27:41] Maya: Great. Any final questions?

[00:27:44] Jamal: Timeline — can you start the config within a week?

[00:27:47] Maya: Yes, we'll share initial artifacts in 3 business days.

[00:27:52] Evelyn: Also need a security addendum for snapshots.

[00:27:55] Maya: We'll attach that too.

[00:28:00] [wrap-up small talk and thanks]

[00:28:12] End of recording
